answers: The Trump Administration submitted to Congress its FY2019 budget request on February 12, 2018. The proposal included $41.86 billion for the Department of State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs (SFOPS). Of that amount, $13.26 billion was for State Department operations, international broadcasting, and related agencies, and $28.60 billion for foreign operations. With the enactment of the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2018 (BBA; P.L. 115-123, February 9, 2018), which raised discretionary spending limits set by the Budget Control Act of 2011 (BCA; P.L. 112-25), the Administration's FY2019 foreign affairs funding request was entirely within enduring (base) funds; no Overseas Contingency Operations (OCO) funding was included the SFOPS request for the first time since FY2012. The FY2019 request would have represented a 23.3% decrease in SFOPS funding compared with FY2018 actual funding levels. The proposed State and related agency funding would have been 18.7% below FY2018 funding and the foreign operations funding would have been reduced by 25.2%. In the State and related programs budget, cuts were proposed for several accounts, including the diplomatic security accounts, contributions to international organizations, and contributions for international peacekeeping activities. In the foreign operations budget, cuts would have been applied across all accounts, with disproportionately large cuts proposed for humanitarian assistance, multilateral assistance, and funding for bilateral development programs focused on agriculture, education, and democracy promotion. Both the House and Senate appropriations committees approved FY2019 SFOPS bills that included funding at higher levels than the Administration requested and closer to FY2018 funding. H.R. 6385, approved by the House appropriations committee on June 20, 2018, would have funded SFOPS accounts at $54.177 billion. S. 3108, approved by the Senate appropriations committee on June 21, 2018, would have provided $54.602 billion for SFOPS accounts. FY2019 began with seven appropriations bills, including SFOPS, unfinished. Congress and the President approved continuing resolutions to fund the affected federal agencies through December 21, 2018 at the FY2018 level (P.L. 115-245, Division C and P.L. 115-298). After December 21, a partial shutdown of the government, including SFOPS funded agencies, occurred. On January 25, 2019, an agreement was reached to continue funding for SFOPS and other appropriations that had lapsed through February 15, at the FY2018 level (P.L. 116-5). On February 14, Congress passed, and the President later signed into law, a full year omnibus appropriation that included SFOPS funding (P.L. 116-6, Division F). P.L. 116-6 included a total of $54.377 billion for SFOPS accounts in FY2019, a 0.3% decrease from the FY2018 funding level and about 30% more than the Administration's request. Of that enacted total, $8.0 billion, or 14.7%, was designated as OCO. This report provides an account-by-account comparison of the FY2019 SFOPS request, House and Senate SFOPS legislation and the final FY2019 SFOPS appropriation to FY2018 funding in Appendix A. The International Affairs (function 150) budget in Appendix B provides a similar comparison. This report will not be further updated unless there is further congressional activity on FY2019 appropriations.

**Summary of FY2019 SFOPS Budget Report**

On February 12, 2018, the Trump Administration submitted its FY2019 budget request to Congress, seeking $41.86 billion for the Department of State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs (SFOPS). This request represented a 23.3% decrease from FY2018 actual funding levels, driven by a 25.2% cut to foreign operations and an 18.7% reduction to State Department operations. The Administration proposed significant structural changes, including the elimination of several accounts (such as the Development Assistance and International Organizations & Programs accounts) and the consolidation of the Overseas Private Investment Corporation and USAID’s Development Credit Authority into a new Development Finance Institution.

Following the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2018, which raised discretionary spending caps, Congress ultimately enacted the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2019 (P.L. 116-6) on February 15. This legislation provided $54.38 billion for SFOPS, a 0.3% decrease from FY2018 and approximately 30% higher than the Administration's request. The enacted bill rejected most of the Administration's proposed account mergers and eliminations, maintaining funding for the Inter-American Foundation and U.S.-Africa Development Foundation at FY2018 levels.

The final appropriation focused on maintaining core diplomatic and security functions. For the State Department, funding for Diplomatic Programs increased to $9.17 billion, a 4% increase over FY2018, which included $2.63 billion for Worldwide Security Protection (WSP) and $1.98 billion for Embassy Security, Construction, and Maintenance (ESCM). The enacted legislation also mandated oversight of State Department personnel levels, requiring the Secretary to report on workforce staffing to prevent reductions below December 31, 2017, levels.

Regarding foreign operations, the enacted bill provided $37.92 billion, including $3.63 billion designated as Overseas Contingency Operations (OCO). While the Administration requested deep cuts to global health and humanitarian assistance, the final bill increased funding for global health to $8.84 billion and humanitarian assistance to $9.53 billion, nearly matching FY2018 levels. Security assistance funding was also increased to $9.15 billion, with specific allocations for key allies like Israel and Egypt, and increased funding for the International Narcotics Control and Law Enforcement (INCLE) account to address opioid flows.

On February 12, 2018, the Trump Administration submitted a FY2019 budget request to Congress for the Department of State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs (SFOPS). The request totaled $41.86 billion, representing a 23.3% decrease from FY2018 actual funding levels. This included $13.26 billion for State operations and $28.60 billion for foreign operations. Consequently, the Administration moved $3.69 billion in Overseas Contingency Operations (OCO) funds into the base budget. Of this total, $16.46 billion was for State Department operations and $37.92 billion for foreign operations, with $8.0 billion designated as OCO.

This included $9.17 billion for the Diplomatic Programs account, $4.10 billion for Worldwide Security Protection, and $1.98 billion for Embassy Security, Construction, and Maintenance. The legislation also included oversight provisions regarding personnel levels and the State Department's "Redesign" modernization efforts.
